These are the solutions to the worksheet of lab 10, section by section. The
👀 *Together* sections repeat the code from class with the explanations; the
✍️ *Your turn* sections show the filled-in code and the answers. Every number
quoted in the [lecture on regression analysis](/content/lecture/l_10_Regression.qmd)
appears somewhere below.

# Setup 👀

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)  # readr, dplyr, ggplot2, purrr
library(broom)      # tidy(), glance(), augment()
```

```{r}
#| label: fmt
#| include: false

# numbers in the text: fixed decimals, typographic minus
fmt <- function(x, d = 0) sub("-", "−", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data-shown
#| eval: false

cps <- read_csv("data/cps-earnings-mra-2014.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| echo: false
#| message: false

cps <- read_csv("../data/cps-earnings-mra-2014.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: prepare-data

cps <- cps |>
  mutate(
    female  = as.integer(sex == 2),             # 1 = woman, 0 = man
    gender  = factor(if_else(female == 1, "Women", "Men")),
    college = as.integer(grade92 >= 43),        # 1 = at least a Bachelor's degree
    edu_cat = factor(
      case_when(grade92 < 43 ~ "No degree",
                grade92 == 43 ~ "Bachelor",
                TRUE ~ "Graduate"),
      levels = c("No degree", "Bachelor", "Graduate")
    )
  )
glimpse(cps)
```

The data contain `r nrow(cps)` market research analysts, `r sum(cps$female)`
of them women.

---

# Part 1: Simple regression in six steps

**Question:** How are weekly earnings related to age?

## 1.1 Explore 👀

```{r}
#| label: scatter

ggplot(cps, aes(x = age, y = earnwke)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Weekly earnings (USD)")
```

```{r}
#| label: ceiling

max(cps$earnwke)
sum(cps$earnwke == max(cps$earnwke))
```

```{r}
#| label: histograms
#| fig-height: 3.5

ggplot(cps, aes(x = earnwke)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25)

ggplot(cps, aes(x = log(earnwke))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25)
```

- The relationship is positive, but weak and noisy.
- Earnings stop at `r fmt(max(cps$earnwke))` USD: the CPS top-codes high
  earnings, and `r sum(cps$earnwke == max(cps$earnwke))` analysts sit at
  this ceiling.
- Earnings are right-skewed; in logs, the distribution is *more* symmetric —
  not perfectly: now the left tail is longer, and the ceiling is still there.

## 1.2 Estimate 👀

```{r}
#| label: slr

m1 <- lm(earnwke ~ age, data = cps)
tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE)
glance(m1)$r.squared
```

- **Slope:** `r fmt(coef(m1)[["age"]], 1)` — analysts who are one year
  older earn, *on average*, about 14 USD more per week. This compares people
  of different ages; it is neither causal nor about any individual.
- **Standard error** `r fmt(tidy(m1)$std.error[2], 1)`, **95% CI**
  [`r fmt(confint(m1)["age", 1], 1)`, `r fmt(confint(m1)["age", 2], 1)`]:
  the slope is clearly different from zero.
- **R²** = `r fmt(glance(m1)$r.squared, 3)`: age alone describes little of
  the variation in earnings. R² says nothing about whether the slope is right,
  and nothing about how well we would predict new analysts.

## 1.3 Diagnose 👀

```{r}
#| label: slr-diagnose

augment(m1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE)
```

The residuals show a hump: the straight line is too low in the middle and
too high at both ends. Back to specifying the model.

## 1.4 Your turn ✍️ — age² and logs

**a.** `I()` makes R compute the square before the formula is read; `age^2`
without `I()` would silently be the same as `age`.

```{r}
#| label: quadratic

m2 <- lm(earnwke ~ age + I(age^2), data = cps)
tidy(m2)
```

**b.**

```{r}
#| label: quadratic-diagnose

augment(m2) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE)
```

The hump has gone. The diagonal stripe at the top right are the top-coded
analysts.

**c.**

```{r}
#| label: slope-at-age

b <- coef(m2)
slope_at <- function(a) b[["age"]] + 2 * b[["I(age^2)"]] * a
slope_at(c(30, 45, 60))
```

About +42 USD per year at 30, +7 at 45 and −27 at 60. The coefficient of
`age` on its own (`r fmt(b[["age"]], 1)`) is the slope at age 0 —
meaningless here. Predicted earnings peak at
$-\hat\beta_1 / 2\hat\beta_2$ ≈ `r fmt(-b[["age"]] / (2 * b[["I(age^2)"]]))` years.

**d.**

```{r}
#| label: log-model

m_log <- lm(log(earnwke) ~ age, data = cps)
tidy(m_log)
```

In a log–level model, 100 × the coefficient is (approximately) the
percentage change: one year of age goes with about
`r fmt(100 * coef(m_log)[["age"]], 1)` % higher earnings.

---

# Part 2: Multiple regression

**Question:** Do women earn less?

## 2.1 The raw gap, and holding hours constant 👀

```{r}
#| label: group-means

cps |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarise(n = n(), earnings = mean(earnwke), hours = mean(uhours))
```

```{r}
#| label: gaps

m_gap   <- lm(earnwke ~ female, data = cps)
m_hours <- lm(earnwke ~ female + uhours, data = cps)
tidy(m_gap)
tidy(m_hours)
```

- The coefficient of a 0/1 variable is the difference in means:
  `r fmt(coef(m_gap)[["female"]])` USD. The intercept is the mean of the men.
- Among analysts working the same hours, the gap shrinks to
  `r fmt(coef(m_hours)[["female"]])` USD (SE `r fmt(tidy(m_hours)$std.error[2])`).

```{r}
#| label: decomposition

delta <- coef(lm(uhours ~ female, data = cps))[["female"]]
delta

coef(m_hours)[["female"]] + coef(m_hours)[["uhours"]] * delta
```

Women work `r fmt(-delta, 1)` hours less, and each hour pays about
`r fmt(coef(m_hours)[["uhours"]], 1)` USD: −218 = −69 + 40.9 × (−3.66).
Which number answers "Do women earn less?" depends on the question. The
**total** effect (−218) includes the path via hours; the **direct** effect
(−69) compares equal hours. If fewer hours are themselves a result of norms
or penalties, controlling for them removes part of what we want to measure.

## 2.2 Your turn ✍️ — model (3)

**a.**

```{r}
#| label: model-3

m3 <- lm(earnwke ~ female + uhours + age + I(age^2) + college, data = cps)
tidy(m3)
glance(m3) |> select(r.squared, adj.r.squared)
```

**b.**

```{r}
#| label: compare-gap

list(`(1) raw` = m_gap, `(2) + hours` = m_hours, `(3) + age, college` = m3) |>
  map_dfr(\(m) tidy(m) |> filter(term == "female"), .id = "model") |>
  select(model, estimate, std.error)
```

The gap in model (3) is `r fmt(coef(m3)[["female"]])` USD with a standard
error of `r fmt(tidy(m3)$std.error[2])` — the 95% CI includes zero: with 252
analysts, we cannot tell it apart from no gap.

## 2.3 ⭐ Your turn — model (4) in logs

**a.**

```{r}
#| label: diagnose-3
#| fig-height: 3.5

augment(m3) |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line()
```

The upper tail lies above the line: the residuals are right-skewed.

**b.**

```{r}
#| label: model-4
#| fig-height: 3.5

m4 <- lm(log(earnwke) ~ female + log(uhours) + age + I(age^2) + college, data = cps)
tidy(m4)

augment(m4) |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line()
```

- The residuals of model (4) are close to normal; R² rises from
  `r fmt(glance(m3)$r.squared, 2)` to `r fmt(glance(m4)$r.squared, 2)`.
- **Gap:** `r fmt(coef(m4)[["female"]], 3)` → about
  `r fmt(100 * (exp(coef(m4)[["female"]]) - 1))` % (exact:
  $e^{\hat\beta} - 1$), again not distinguishable from zero.
- **Hours** (log–log): an elasticity of
  `r fmt(coef(m4)[["log(uhours)"]], 1)` — 1 % more hours go with about 1.3 %
  higher earnings.

---

# Part 3: Groups and interactions

## 3.1 Reference groups and interactions 👀

```{r}
#| label: education

m_edu <- lm(earnwke ~ female + uhours + age + I(age^2) + edu_cat, data = cps)
tidy(m_edu)

cps_b <- cps |> mutate(edu_cat = relevel(edu_cat, ref = "Bachelor"))
lm(earnwke ~ female + uhours + age + I(age^2) + edu_cat, data = cps_b) |>
  tidy()
```

R uses the first level of a factor as the reference group. Compared with
analysts without a degree: Bachelor's +`r fmt(coef(m_edu)[["edu_catBachelor"]])`,
graduate degree +`r fmt(coef(m_edu)[["edu_catGraduate"]])` USD. With
`relevel()`, the same model compares with Bachelor's instead: graduate vs
Bachelor's ≈ +285 USD.

```{r}
#| label: par-int

m_par <- lm(earnwke ~ age + female, data = cps)
m_int <- lm(earnwke ~ age * female, data = cps)
tidy(m_int)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-par-int
#| fig-height: 3.5

bind_rows(
  augment(m_par, data = cps) |> mutate(model = "Parallel slopes"),
  augment(m_int, data = cps) |> mutate(model = "Interaction")
) |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, colour = gender)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = earnwke), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted), linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~model)
```

Slopes: men `r fmt(coef(m_int)[["age"]], 1)`, women
`r fmt(coef(m_int)[["age"]] + coef(m_int)[["age:female"]], 1)`. The
difference (`r fmt(coef(m_int)[["age:female"]], 1)`, SE
`r fmt(tidy(m_int)$std.error[4], 1)`) is not precisely estimated.

## 3.2 Your turn ✍️ — centring

```{r}
#| label: centring

m_int40 <- lm(earnwke ~ I(age - 40) * female, data = cps)
tidy(m_int40)
```

```{r}
#| label: centring-30-50

map_dbl(c(30, 40, 50), \(a) coef(lm(earnwke ~ I(age - a) * female, data = cps))[["female"]])
```

Same model, same fit — only the meaning of the `female` coefficient changes:
it is the gap at the age we measure from. Gap at 30: about −149, at 40:
`r fmt(coef(m_int40)[["female"]])`, at 50: about −293 USD.

## 3.3 ⭐ Your turn — plot the gap by age

```{r}
#| label: gap-by-age

gap_by_age <- map_dfr(seq(25, 60, by = 5), \(a) {
  lm(earnwke ~ I(age - a) * female, data = cps) |>
    tidy(conf.int = TRUE) |>
    filter(term == "female") |>
    mutate(age = a)
})

ggplot(gap_by_age, aes(x = age, y = estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line()
```

The gap widens with age, but the band is wide: it includes zero at the
youngest ages (up to about 34), and only just excludes it at 60.

---

# Summary: the six steps

| Step | What we did |
|:--|:--|
| **Question** | Do earnings rise with age? Do women earn less — and why? |
| **Explore** | Weak, hump-shaped age profile · skew · ceiling · women work fewer hours |
| **Specify** | Age² · logs · hours: total or direct effect? · interaction age × female |
| **Estimate** | `lm()` · slope 14.4 · gap −218 raw, −69 to −83 with controls, ≈ −5 % in logs |
| **Diagnose** | `augment()`: hump → age² · heavy right tail → logs · top-coding |
| **Interpret** | Gap mostly linked to hours · not causal · imprecise with n = 252 |
